vignette:
Ben traces the clean, minimalist lines on the blueprint with a finger that slightly trembles. For his clients, he creates spaces of light and flow, sanctuaries of glass and open air meant to soothe the soul. He is known for his ability to transform a room, to imbue it with a sense of peace and security. His own home, however, has not been a sanctuary for a very long time.

It’s been four years since the night the glass shattered. He and his wife, Elara, had been watching a film in the living room he’d designed to be their haven—warm woods, soft fabrics, art from their travels across the Pacific. The sound was like a gunshot, a violent tearing of the fabric of their world. Before he could even rise from the sofa, two men were on them. The memory isn’t a linear story anymore; it’s a collage of sensory tortures. The acrid smell of stale cigarette smoke on their clothes, the rough scrape of the zip ties on his wrists, the cold dread that flooded his body as he watched them shove Elara into a corner. He remembers the feeling of the carpet fibers pressed against his cheek, the muffled sound of their ransacking, and the chilling, quiet way they spoke to each other as if he and his wife were merely furniture.

In the weeks that followed, Elara was the strong one. She insisted they stay in the house. “We won’t let them take this from us, too,” she’d said, her voice firm, even as her hands shook while she brewed tea. Ben said nothing, but he began changing the space. He replaced the beautiful floor-to-ceiling windows with smaller, reinforced ones. He installed a security system with so many sensors that the house felt more like a vault than a home. He, the master of open-plan living, began to close doors.

Elara’s cancer diagnosis came a year later, an entirely separate violence that felt, to Ben, like a delayed aftershock of that night. As she grew weaker, his vigilance grew stronger. He’d lie awake for hours, listening to the house settle, his body rigid, convinced every creak was an intruder. He saw the world outside as a place of relentless threat, and his role was to keep it from breaching the walls again. He failed to protect Elara from the men; he would not fail to protect her from the world. But he couldn't protect her from the illness inside her.

Since her passing two years ago, the house has become his tomb. The living room, their shared space of terror, is permanently dark, the heavy curtains he installed always drawn. He lives and works out of his small office and the kitchen. He eats standing up, quickly, as if ready to flee. His grown children call, their voices laced with a concern he can’t bring himself to acknowledge. They invite him for dinner, for holidays with his grandchildren, but the thought of leaving the house after dusk fills him with a suffocating panic.

At work, the mask of the accomplished designer is harder to maintain. He finds himself fixating on security—suggesting deadbolts and window bars to clients who just want a new color palette. During a consultation last month, a client’s husband dropped a book, and Ben flinched so violently he knocked over a tray of paint samples. The couple stared, their polite smiles frozen. He mumbled an apology about low blood sugar, the shame hot on his face.

Now, in the quiet of his fortified home, he looks at the plans for a client’s sun-drenched atrium. He can still conceptualize beauty, order, and safety for others. He can draw the lines, choose the materials, and imagine a family living there in blissful peace. But when he lifts his head and looks around his own darkened room, the silence isn’t peaceful. It’s heavy, listening, waiting for the sound of breaking glass. The thought, a familiar poison, seeps in: *A man protects his wife. A man protects his home. You did neither.* He closes his eyes, but the image of the men’s faces is already there, waiting for him in the dark.
